title: AKS: Azure Kubernetes Service Operations
intro: AKS is Azure's managed Kubernetes. Once you're connected, it's ordinary kubectl (see the Kubernetes category). The Azure-specific parts are getting credentials safely, node pools, and upgrades, which Azure performs but you have to plan.

steps.prompt: List the AKS clusters in the subscription.
steps.fake_output:
Name          Location    ResourceGroup  KubernetesVersion  ProvisioningState
------------  ----------  -------------  -----------------  -----------------
aks-prod      westeurope  rg-aks-prod    1.29.7             Succeeded
aks-staging   westeurope  rg-aks-stg     1.30.3             Succeeded
steps.explanation: Prod is one minor version behind staging.
steps.why: Running staging a version ahead of prod, and upgrading staging first, is the standard way to catch API removals before they hit production.

steps.prompt: Get credentials for aks-staging (rg-aks-stg). Only staging for now.
steps.explanation: A context for aks-staging was added AND made current.
steps.why: 'as current context' is the warning to notice. get-credentials silently switches kubectl to the cluster you just fetched, and it's the start of azure-incident-005. Check with 'kubectl config current-context' after every get-credentials.

steps.prompt: List the node pools of aks-prod (rg-aks-prod).
expected_commands: az aks nodepool list --resource-group rg-aks-prod --cluster-name aks-prod --output table
az aks nodepool list -g rg-aks-prod --cluster-name aks-prod -o table
steps.fake_output:
Name      OsType  VmSize            Count  Mode    OrchestratorVersion
--------  ------  ----------------  -----  ------  -------------------
system    Linux   Standard_D4s_v5   3      System  1.29.7
workload  Linux   Standard_D8s_v5   6      User    1.29.7
gpu       Linux   Standard_NC6s_v3  0      User    1.29.7
steps.explanation: A system pool for cluster components, a workload pool, and a GPU pool scaled to zero.
steps.why: Keep system components (CoreDNS, metrics-server) on a small dedicated System pool so a runaway application can't starve them. A pool scaled to 0 costs nothing until the cluster autoscaler needs it.

steps.prompt: Check which Kubernetes versions aks-prod (rg-aks-prod) can upgrade to.
expected_commands: az aks get-upgrades --resource-group rg-aks-prod --name aks-prod --output table
az aks get-upgrades -g rg-aks-prod -n aks-prod -o table
steps.fake_output:
Name     ResourceGroup  MasterVersion  Upgrades
-------  -------------  -------------  --------------
default  rg-aks-prod    1.29.7         1.30.3, 1.30.4
steps.explanation: One minor version up is available: 1.30.
steps.why: Kubernetes upgrades go one minor version at a time. Before upgrading, check for deprecated APIs your manifests still use (tools like kubent or pluto), and set a PodDisruptionBudget for critical apps so node drains stay graceful (see incident-012 for a PDB that blocks forever).

steps.prompt: Upgrade aks-prod (rg-aks-prod) to 1.30.4, control plane and node pools together.
steps.fake_output:
Kubernetes may be unavailable during cluster upgrades.
Are you sure you want to perform this operation? (y/N): y
Since control-plane-only argument is not specified, this will upgrade the control plane AND all nodepools to version 1.30.4. Continue? (y/N): y
(upgrade in progress: nodes are surged, cordoned, drained, and replaced one by one)
steps.explanation: AKS upgrades the control plane, then replaces nodes using a surge (an extra node at a time by default).
steps.why: Node pools upgrade with a surge-and-drain: a new node is added, an old one drained and removed. Increasing max-surge speeds up big pools at the cost of temporary extra capacity. Upgrade staging first, and schedule prod upgrades in AKS maintenance windows.
